ground_truth.title: Beginner woodworking projects
ground_truth.author: JWoodguy13
ground_truth.main_content:
Hello all,
New here and keen to get into the woodworking hobby properly. ATM I only have basic power tools (hoping to expand range) which are:
Jigsaw
Circular saw
Battery Drill
Angle grinder
Stick welder
Power Drill
Orbital sander
As well as the normal everyday hand tools. I was wondering if anyone had any good begginers projects up their sleeves that ae fun to make. Currently working on a side table with metal legs and wooden top, but want something to move onto after tge current project. Any suggestions would be appreciated.

It would be a definite plus if you can get a decent table saw, not a jobsite saw and decent routers.
Pretty much everything needs a table saw. Combined with what you already have, quite a bit can be done. For example, if you wanted a table top with rounded corners, your jig saw will be used to rough cut the curve and the angle grinder with anywhere from 25 to 40 grit sanding disk will easily sculpt the curve nice and even. Then a router can 'ease over' the top edges. Table legs and aprons are also easy to make with a table saw.
For most woodworkers. the table saw is the heart of their operation so dont cheap-0ut.

Think small and work your way up, nothing can be more discouraging than spending a few hundred on material and finding things just didn't work out as you planned, one example is the number inquiries here on how to fix a table that was a first time project. It is a hobby and it should be fun, so enjoy the journey one step at a time.
I haven't done my housekeeping with the links lately, but there are some ideas here:
Absolutely Free Plans Index

Thanks for your help...in regards to getting a table saw at this stage I just want to try out the hobby and make sure it is really for me before I start getting the bigger and more expensive tools. But is something I would like to get in the future.

Carpenter's tool box, bird house, bat house, napkin holder, foot stool, side table, magazine rack (LOL - yeah, magazines... sorry, I'm old), coin box (covered or not).

Have fun! Be careful, read the manuals on every tool you own so you know the good and bad.

Thanks Domo there's some good suggestions there 👍

Cribbage board! (Thought of that last night before going to bed.)

4-across game, Tic-Tac-Toe box with X and O and playing surface.

Gifts for significant other and family. Especially the significant other who may have veto power over tool purchases.

I did a web search for "woodworking projects for teens" and saw lots of good ideas.

@JWoodguy13 welcome to the forum and to woodworking! The others have given some great suggestions, but here's a few more.... paper towel holder, a clock for your shop, candle sconces, planter box, step stool or small bench, picture frames. Also, you could build a decent workbench if you don't have one already.

I started out with pretty much the same tool set you have. But I also had a router, a Stanley #5 hand plane, a couple of chisels, 1 hard-point backsaw, and some pipe clamps. I agree with @Tony B that you'll soon want a router for edge work and cutting dadoes, grooves, and rabbets. And if you don't have a decent hand plane, I recommend you get one and learn how to sharpen/use it. You'll want it to smooth out surfaces and the tool marks left by your saws. You can get a decent Stanley #5 cheap enough on eBay, but get one that's pretty much ready to use unless you think you'd be interested in restoring a neglected one.

Have fun, be safe, and remember to post pics of the stuff you make.

Thanks everyone for your suggestions. @NormL I already have a hand plane which I am still trying to learn how to use, but I was wondering if an electric hand plane would be easier and can used instead?

JW13,
Check out Rex Kreuger's videos on YouTube. He makes some neat projects with way less tools than you have.

Have fun! Be careful, read the manuals on every tool you own so you know the good and bad.

Please continue learning to use the hand plane. There's a lot of good videos out there on how to set it up and use it. Paul Sellers and Rob Cosman among several others. Even if you primarily use power tools, you will find that hand tool skills are indispensable and will become your best friends.

An electric hand planer is certainly easier to use from an effort standpoint, but it's really only useful for removing a lot of wood from the face of a board. But in that case, you're better off saving up to get a lunchbox planer. The electric hand planer cannot replace a hand plane. It's awkward to use on edges and you can't use it on end grain.

As a newcomer to the hobby, I suggest that you wait and see if you really need one. This hobby is expensive enough just to get the things you really need. Don't be in a hurry to get tools that you think you need. You'll be amazed at what you can do with the tools you already have.

Thanks everyone will check out the people you suggested
